strategies.label: Single agent
strategies.description: One agent, one context, the full toolset. It reads the task, acts, and answers in a single session with no separate planning, review or delegation step. This is the control condition the other architectures are measured against: every extra phase they add has to earn its cost and latency back in score.

strategies.label: Plan then execute
strategies.description: The run is split in two: a tool-less planning call writes an ordered list of steps, then a second call executes them with the full toolset. The planner cannot look anything up, so the plan is only as good as the task statement — the question this architecture answers is whether committing to a sequence up front beats deciding one action at a time.

strategies.label: Orchestrator with parallel workers
strategies.description: An orchestrator splits the task into independent subtasks, fans them out to workers that run at the same time in separate contexts, then writes the answer from their reports. It trades wall-clock time for coordination risk: the workers cannot see each other, so anything the split gets wrong — an overlap, a dependency, a missing piece — shows up in the score. When the orchestrator judges that the task cannot honestly be split, one worker is given the whole task, so the architecture reduces to a single agent with an orchestrator around it.

strategies.label: Plan, execute, verify, revise
strategies.description: Plan, execute, then hand the work to a verifier that holds only the read-only tools and has to check the real state rather than the executor's account of it. A rejection with a blocking issue goes back for revision, at most twice; one with only minor issues ends the review, since a full revision over a detail risks more than it fixes. It is the most expensive way to buy a second opinion, and the measurement is whether catching the executor's mistakes is worth what the review costs.

strategies.label: Parallel proposals, select, execute
strategies.description: Three proposers investigate the task in parallel with read-only tools, each starting from a different angle — the rules, the current state, the outcome the user needs — and each returns a course of action; a selector picks the strongest and merges in what the others got right; a final call applies it with the full toolset. Nothing is changed until one approach has been chosen, which is the point: it spends three investigations to avoid committing to the first idea. The proposers never see one another, so this is selection among independent proposals, not a debate. On a task with nothing to mutate the selector's merged answer is the answer.

strategies.label: Execute with action review
strategies.description: One executor with the full toolset, but every call it makes that would change state is first put to a reviewer: a separate, read-only call that holds the domain policy, checks the current state and allows or denies the action. A denial comes back to the executor as the tool's result, with the reason, so it can adapt; reads pass straight through. It is review at the point of action rather than after the fact — it can stop a mistake before it lands instead of trying to undo it — and the measurement is whether that is worth a model call per action. On a task with nothing to change there is nothing to review, and it runs exactly as a single agent.
